opening.headline: Let's explore how agents developed by different organizations delegate tasks and receive results using the A2A protocol.
body: Consider a scenario where an agent from one company needs to delegate work to an agent from another company. The two agents differ in their framework, language, and vendor. They cannot access each other's internal tools or memories. Yet, they must still discover what the other can do and exchange updates on the progress of lengthy tasks.

The A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol is a specification that defines how independent agents communicate and collaborate like peers. This course examines the core concepts and message flow of A2A, distinguishes between the MCP (Middleware Connectivity Protocol) used to connect tools and the division of roles, and finally reviews the agent gateway that controls connections across organizational boundaries.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the core concepts of A2A (Agent Card, Task, Message, Part, Artifact) and the role differences between A2A and MCP.
It is possible to distinguish between the points where MCP can be applied and where A2A can be applied within the given connectivity requirements.

screens.title: How do agents from different organizations collaborate?
screens.lead: Review the scenario where a facility agent needs to place a part order with a supplier agent from another company. Check what difficulties may arise, along with the accompanying diagram.

visual.alt: Diagram showing agents from the maintenance organization and agents from the supplier organization meeting across different organizational boundaries.
labels: ① What can the other party do?
② What is the status of a task that takes a long time?
③ How can trust be established without disclosing the internal details?
Internal tools and memory are private

paragraphs: The repair shop agent determined after completing the diagnosis of the customer's vehicle that part #12345 is required. However, this part is supplied by an agent from another company. The repair shop agent must place an order for this part.

Two agents were built using different frameworks, different languages, and different vendors. They cannot access each other's internal tools or memories, and should not be allowed to do so. In this state, collaboration is possible only if the agents can answer three key questions.

First, how do we determine what actions a counterpart agent is capable of performing? Second, how do we exchange updates on the progress of long-running operations? Third, how can we communicate in a way that is trustworthy without exposing internal implementations?

The A2A protocol is a specification designed to bridge this gap. It defines the manner in which agents from different sources discover each other, negotiate, share tasks, and exchange context and complex data at the application layer.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Should standardized tools with defined inputs and outputs, as well as autonomous agents that plan and query independently, be connected to agents using the same method? This class distinguishes between these differences.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the differences we already know between MCP and A2A.

screens.title: Preview: How is MCP different from A2A?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think through your answer mentally before clicking it.

items.prompt: Is a calculator and database query API a "tool" or a "agent"?
items.answer: Both are clearly input-output functions, generally stateless, thus resembling tools. Upon invocation, they return a result in a predefined format. It is within the MCP's domain to define how such functions are connected to agents.

items.prompt: When delegating a task to an agent from another team, do we need to know their tool list?
items.answer: There is no need to know, and nothing can be known, according to principle. The other party is a black box that operates without revealing its internal tools or memory. What I need to know consists solely of the capabilities declared by the other party, and the messages exchanged and their outcomes.

items.prompt: If a task that takes several hours is assigned, where should its status be recorded?
items.answer: A single temporary response is insufficient. A task unit with a unique ID and state is required, and the lifecycle—such as in progress, additional input needed, or completed—must be tracked. In A2A, this is referred to as a Task.

screens.outro: Let us compare the thought that comes to mind with the core concept of A2A.

screens.title: A2A's core concept: Actors and five elements
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms highlighted below, a description appears above them. Please review the terms one by one.

visual.alt: User, A2A client, A2A server interacting, with the server interior represented as a black box in a diagram of actors.
labels: Internal tools and memory are not visible (black box)

data.text: There are three types of participants in A2A. The user is the entity that initiates a request, either a human or an automated service. The A2A client is an agent that starts communication on behalf of the user. The A2A server is a remote agent that exposes an HTTP endpoint implementing A2A, and to the client it appears as an internal entity that is not visible—specifically, black box. Communication involves five fundamental elements. Agent Card is a JSON document that functions as a digital business card, containing an agent's identity, capabilities, endpoint, skills, and authentication requirements, serving as the starting point for discovery. Task is a stateful work unit with a unique identifier and a defined lifetime. Message represents a turn between the client and the agent, with the role being either user or agent. Part is the minimal content unit that contains one of text, file reference, or structured data within Message or Artifact. Artifact is a concrete output produced by an agent during a workflow, which may be a document, image, or structured data, and can be streamed progressively.

terms.tip: This means that the internal operations, memory, and tools of the remote agent are not visible to the client. This is also known as opaque execution. The client knows only the declared capabilities and the exchanged results.

A JSON metadata document containing an agent's identity, capabilities, endpoints, skills, and authentication requirements. The client reads this document to determine whether the agent is suitable for a task and how to securely request it.
An agent-initiated work unit in a started state. It possesses a unique ID and a predefined lifetime, enabling tracking of long-running tasks and collaborations spanning multiple turns.

This is a single communication between a client and an agent. It carries a role (either user or agent) and a unique messageId, transmitting instructions, context, questions, answers, and state updates.

The smallest unit that contains actual content within a Message or Artifact. A single Part contains exactly one of the following: text, a file reference (URL or inline bytes), or structured data. As a result, A2A is not bound to any specific format.
This is a concrete output created by the agent during execution. Examples include documents, images, and structured data; the result is delivered in a structured format that can be retrieved again.

screens.outro: Having verified the elements, I will now proceed step by step to trace how these elements connect within the actual flow.

screens.title: Message flow from Agent Card to Task completion
screens.lead: Follow the workflow where the maintenance agent assigns lengthy tasks to the vendor agent. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

visual.alt: Sequence diagram showing agent card retrieval between client and server, message transmission, task response, additional input, termination, and artifact delivery.
labels: Task creation (taskId, contextId) status: In progress

steps.title: Step 1: Discovery
steps.body: The client first reads the opposing agent's Agent Card to determine whether the agent is suitable for the task and how to securely request it. The Agent Card contains information such as identity, endpoint, skills, and authentication requirements, allowing the client to match an appropriate authentication method before sending the request.

steps.title: Step 2: Request
steps.body: The client sends a message. If the agent can respond immediately, it responds with a Message; if the task takes time, it responds with a Task. A parts order requires inventory verification and shipping preparation, so a Task is created.

steps.title: Step 3: Proceed
steps.body: Tasks are associated with a taskId and a contextId. The taskId refers to the specific task, while the contextId groups related tasks and messages into a single conversation context. There are three methods to check task progress: polling, where the client periodically queries; server-sent events (SSE) streaming, which provides real-time updates over an open HTTP connection; and push notifications, where the server calls a webhook specified by the client. Push notifications are appropriate for long-running tasks or when clients have disconnected connections.

steps.title: Step 4: Additional Input
steps.body: If the agent requires more information, change the Task status to input-required. For example, if the agent requests confirmation of quantity. The client then sends a new message with the same taskId and contextId to continue. This enables collaborative interactions across multiple turns to occur within a single Task.

steps.title: Step 5: Termination and Outputs
steps.body: completed, failed, canceled, rejected are terminal states. Once a task reaches a terminal state, it can no longer receive messages. The result of the task is delivered as an Artifact. For example, an order confirmation becomes an Artifact. If additional work is required, create a new task while preserving the context via the same contextId.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the A2A flow, let's compare how MCP and A2A divide their respective roles.

screens.title: A2A and MCP: Vertical and Horizontal
screens.lead: Alternate between the two states and compare the difference in direction and target between MCP and A2A.

states.label: MCP: Vertical (depth)
states.body:
MCP deepens an agent's capabilities. It connects the tools, resources, and skills an agent uses within a single application. Every additional MCP connection enables the agent to perform more tasks.

Targets are typically functions with clear inputs and outputs and no state. Examples include calculators, database query APIs, and weather lookup services. The agent uses tools to gather information and perform individual functions. Since the model directly calls tools, a single agent becomes capable of performing more tasks on its own. To put it simply, it's like giving a person a new tool.

states.label: A2A: Horizontal (width)
states.body:
A2A connects agents beyond boundaries. The counterpart agent may belong to a different team, department, or collaborating organization. My agent detects the counterpart, negotiates, and exchanges information. Going beyond simply asking for status, it shares context as if a person is seeking help from another, delving deeper or introducing a more suitable agent.

The counterpart independently reasons, plans, uses multiple tools, and maintains state throughout extended interactions. Examples include a customer service agent forwarding an inquiry to a payment agent, or a travel agent coordinating with air, hotel, and activity agents.

screens.outro: Let us consider the scenario at a maintenance facility where both specifications are used together.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Tools are categorized under MCP, and agents under A2A.
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of dividing the four connectivity requirements of logistics systems into MCP and A2A. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

visual.alt: The logistics agent connects to internal tools via MCP and to external organization agents via A2A.
labels: Thick line = Agent connection (assigned to task)

steps.title: Verify the requirements
steps.body: The logistics agent requires four connections: first, querying the inventory database; second, delegating shipments to a third-party logistics agent; third, reading the internal cost sheet; and fourth, requesting approval from an external authentication agent. Rather than considering whether all these can be handled through a single approach, the starting point should be to categorize them based on their respective characteristics.

steps.title: Step 1: Pose the question
steps.body: For each connection, the same question is asked: Is the other party a function with fixed inputs and outputs, or is it a autonomous system that plans independently and has a state? This question serves as the criterion for distinguishing between MCP and A2A.

steps.title: Step 2: Classify
steps.body: Inventory queries and internal unit prices are tools and data with structured inputs and outputs, therefore they are connected via MCP. Delivery outsourcing and approval requests are tasks delegated to agents within other organizations, therefore they are connected via A2A. Approval agents can ask for additional information and maintain the status, making A2A the appropriate choice.

steps.title: Step 3: Design the A2A connection
steps.body: Delivery delegation first verifies the other party's capabilities and authentication requirements using an Agent Card. Then, it delegates the task and tracks delivery progress. If delivery takes several hours or longer, push notifications are more efficient than polling. The final result is received as an Artifact.

steps.title: Step 4: Design the boundary
steps.body: The opposing agent's internal tools and memory are not visible, so there is no basis to trust the opponent's internal operations. Authentication is applied according to the authentication requirements declared by the agent on the Agent Card, and the returned results are validated against this organization's policies. Inter-organizational connections require separate control points. Next, we examine the agent gateway in the following screen.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at what a device that controls connections at the organizational boundary looks like.

screens.title: Manage boundary management using an agent gateway
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore the components that the agent gateway controls. This content is based on the Google Agent Platform documentation.

tabs.label: gateway
tabs.body: Agent Gateway is the network entry and exit point for all interactions involving agents. It handles connections between users and agents, agents and tools, and agents and agents. It manages encrypted connections (mTLS), translates protocols such as MCP, REST, and gRPC, and applies policy checks to all traffic. The key aspect is that policy enforcement is centralized in a single location.

tabs.label: agent id
tabs.body: Each agent is assigned a unique and secure ID. This ID serves as authentication, access control, and audit evidence, similar to a digital signature. It answers the question of "who made the request." The agent ID is fundamentally protected through cryptographic authentication using mTLS and DPoP.

tabs.label: Agent Registry
tabs.body: This is a central list of approved agents, tools, MCP servers, and endpoints within an organization. It answers the question "which destinations are approved?" The gateway verifies permissions against this list before allowing a connection. Agents cannot exit to destinations not listed in this registry.

tabs.label: policy
tabs.body: Defines what actions are allowed. The IAM integrated access policy connects an agent's ID to approved tools and endpoints in the registry, by default blocking all connections and only permitting explicitly allowed paths. Model Armor continuously monitors and validates user prompts and tool responses to prevent prompt injection, sensitive information leakage, and harmful content. Intent-based, natural language policies block unintended behaviors such as unsafe tool combinations at runtime.

screens.outro: We have examined the structure, examples, and control mechanisms. Now, I will summarize one criterion for judgment.

screens.title: A line teaching tools and agents
screens.lead: This summarizes the content reviewed so far as a single evaluation criterion.

paragraphs: MCP handles the internal aspects of a single agent by connecting tools and resources with structured inputs and outputs, adding depth to the agent. A2A handles the external interactions between agents, facilitating collaboration across organizational boundaries in the order of discovery (Agent Card), delegation (Task), and results (Artifact).

The decision criterion is the other party's nature. If the other party has a predefined function, connect via MCP; if the other party is an independent agent with its own planning capabilities and state, connect via A2A. The two complement each other without replacing one another. For example, an A2A server could expose well-defined skills as MCP resources to be used like tools. However, A2A excels in scenarios requiring collaboration and state management.

Sub-agents that communicate rapidly over memory within the same process are closer to internal modules. When dealing with independent services built by different teams, different organizations, or in different languages, consider A2A (application-to-application) communication.

Finally, a gateway device that enforces identity, approval lists, and policies from a single point is needed at the boundary between agents. Since we cannot know the internal state of the other side, control at the boundary becomes even more critical.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The tool connects to MCP, and the agent connects to A2A. MCP adds depth to the agent, while A2A adds breadth among agents.

checks.intro: Now, let's look at the flow you just learned in sequential order. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Let's walk through the workflow where the maintenance agent from A2A assigns lengthy tasks to the vendor agent in sequence.
items: Reads the Agent Card to verify the capabilities and authentication requirements of the opposing agent.
Sends a message; if it takes a long time, the agent responds with a Task.
If more information is needed, it enters the input-required state and sends an additional message with the same taskId.
The process completes in the same terminated state and the output is delivered as an Artifact.
checks.explain: The sequence is: discovery (Agent Card), request and task generation, additional input, termination, and artifact delivery. After the termination state, no further messages can be received.

checks.intro: Think of use cases and pick one. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Which of the following is the appropriate target for connecting via MCP rather than A2A?
options: An internal inventory DB query function with fixed input and output
Outsourcing delivery to an agent of a third-party logistics provider from another organization
External authentication agent that queries for additional information and maintains state
A vendor agent that manages task states without exposing internal implementation
checks.explain: Functions with clear input and output and generally no state are best suited to MCP. Independent agents from other organizations with plans and state are connected via A2A.

wrong.1: Delegating tasks to agents from other organizations falls within the domain of A2A.
wrong.2: Since it is an autonomous system that queries and maintains its state, A2A is appropriate.
wrong.3: Collaboration between a blackbox agent with internal concealment and a Task is A2A.

glossary.def: A JSON metadata document containing an agent's identity, capabilities, endpoint, skills, and authentication requirements, serving as the starting point for clients to discover agents.
A stateful work unit with a unique ID and a lifetime period. Tracks long-running operations and collaborations across multiple turns.
An identifier that groups multiple operations and messages into a single conversation context.
Specific outputs created by the agent during the workflow, such as documents, images, structured data, etc.
It is the entry and exit point for all connections between agents, users, tools, and other agents, and the device that enforces policies.

misconceptions.fact: They complement each other. Tool connection is handled by MCP, while agent collaboration is managed by A2A. It is common to use them together within a single system.

misconceptions.myth: To collaborate with a remote agent, you must share its tools and memory.
misconceptions.fact: Transparency is not a principle. The internal workings of a remote agent are not visible, and only the declared capabilities, exchanged messages, and outputs are available.

misconceptions.myth: A2A requests always receive immediate responses.
misconceptions.fact: If a response can be provided immediately, respond with a Message; if it takes longer, respond with a Task. Progress updates are received via polling, SSE streaming, or push notifications.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Tools connect to MCP, and agents connect via A2A. MCP adds depth to the agent, while A2A adds breadth among agents.
The core of A2A is Agent Card (discovery), Task (a task with a lifecycle), Message·Part·Artifact (communication and outputs).
The remote agent acts as a black box with no internal exposure, so what is needed are only the declared capabilities and exchanged results.
At the organizational boundary, the agent gateway controls connections through identity, approval lists, and policies.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the boundary between agents in my system, and what information crosses that boundary?
